sections.title: 1. Start with uncertainty, not formulas
paragraphs: Probability describes uncertainty about an outcome before we observe it. An experiment is something we can repeat under specified conditions; an outcome is one complete result of one trial. The sample space S contains those atomic outcomes. Events are subsets of S. For a single fair die, S={1,2,3,4,5,6}. The event A="even" is {2,4,6}, so P(A)=3/6. Every expression starts with a modelling choice: what exactly counts as one equally likely atomic outcome?

With two labelled dice, write (die 1, die 2). There are 6×6=36 ordered pairs. The *sums* 2,...,12 are not equally likely because sum 2 is produced only by (1,1), while sum 7 is produced by six pairs. If you assume the eleven sums have equal probability, you are counting the wrong sample space. This distinction underlies many GATE traps. When the problem states "without replacement," probabilities can change between selections. When choices are independent, earlier outcomes do not change later probabilities.

sections.title: 2. The mathematics of sets and events
paragraphs: The union A∪B means A or B (including both); intersection A∩B means A and B; complement Aᶜ means not A. These definitions translate English statements to precise questions. "At least one 6" is the complement of "no 6". For two independent dice, P(at least one 6)=1−(5/6)²=11/36. This is faster than enumerating all eleven ordered pairs, but the enumeration verifies the result.

The three core probability axioms say P(A) is nonnegative, P(S)=1, and mutually exclusive events add. Derived rules include P(Aᶜ)=1−P(A) and P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). The intersection correction prevents counting shared outcomes twice. Be careful: mutually exclusive events have an empty intersection, while independent events generally have a nonzero intersection. Two nonzero-probability events cannot be both disjoint and independent.

sections.title: 3. Conditioning: change the reference population
paragraphs: Conditional probability P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) asks how often A happens *among cases in which B occurred*, provided P(B)>0. Imagine six possible die values and learn the outcome is even. Only {2,4,6} remain possible. Then P(value>3 | even)=2/3. You cannot divide by six anymore. The denominator is now the size or total probability of the restricted space.

Bayes' rule follows by writing the same joint probability in two ways: P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A). Rearranging, P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). In diagnostic testing, P(positive|disease) is sensitivity; P(disease|positive) is positive predictive value. They are not interchangeable. Suppose disease prevalence is 1%, sensitivity 90%, false-positive rate 5%. Of 10,000 individuals, about 90 true positives and 495 false positives occur. Only 90/(90+495)≈15.4% of positive results correspond to disease. The low base rate dominates intuition.

sections.title: 4. Random variables give numbers to outcomes
paragraphs: A random variable X maps each outcome to a numerical value. Discrete X has probability mass function p(x)=P(X=x), whose values sum to 1. Continuous X has probability *density* f(x), whose area under intervals yields probability; P(X=a)=0 for a continuous distribution with a density. The cumulative distribution F(x)=P(X≤x) works for both kinds. For discrete variables F jumps; for continuous densities F is an integral.

Expected value E[X]=Σxp(x) for discrete X, or ∫xf(x)dx for continuous X, is the long-run average over repetitions, not necessarily a realizable outcome. Variance Var(X)=E[(X−E[X])²]=E[X²]−E[X]² measures spread and has squared units. Standard deviation is √variance and returns to the units of X. Covariance Cov(X,Y) tracks joint movements; correlation divides covariance by the two standard deviations to obtain a unit-free quantity in [−1,1]. Zero correlation does *not* imply independence in general.

sections.title: 5. Recognize distributions from stories
paragraphs: A Bernoulli variable represents one binary trial, with mean p and variance p(1−p). A binomial variable counts successes over n independent, equal-p Bernoulli trials; P(X=k)=C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k). A geometric variable counts trials until first success, with P(X=k)=(1−p)^(k−1)p for k=1,2,... . A Poisson variable counts events in a fixed interval with expected count λ, while an exponential variable models waiting time with rate λ and survival P(T>t)=e^(−λt). Do not confuse the exponential *rate* λ with mean waiting time 1/λ.

A normal variable has bell-shaped density determined by mean μ and standard deviation σ. Standardization Z=(X−μ)/σ lets us consult one common standard normal table. The central limit theorem (CLT) says sample means, properly standardized, become approximately normal under suitable conditions as n grows, even when individual observations are not normally distributed. The law of large numbers (LLN) says the sample mean converges toward the population mean; CLT instead describes the distribution of sampling error.

sections.title: 6. Statistics turns samples into conclusions
paragraphs: A statistic is calculated from a sample; a parameter describes the population. If independent observations have variance σ², the sample mean has variance σ²/n and standard error σ/√n. Four times as many observations reduce standard error by a factor of two, not four. When σ is known and the sampling model permits it, an approximate 95% confidence interval is sample_mean ±1.96σ/√n. It is a statement about how the procedure performs over repeated sampling, not a posterior probability for the fixed unknown mean.

In hypothesis testing, specify H0 and H1 before looking at results. A p-value is the probability *under H0* of seeing a statistic at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not P(H0 is true). Rejecting at significance level α means p≤α; failing to reject is not proof H0 is true. Common test families: z for known σ in suitable normal/large-sample settings, t for unknown σ in standard mean tests, and chi-square for categorical count-based association or normal-theory variance inference. Always check assumptions and degrees of freedom.

sections.title: 7. Worked problem: joint probability and conditioning
paragraphs: A bag has three red and two blue balls. Draw two balls without replacement. What is P(both red)? First draw red with probability 3/5. Given that, two red remain among four balls, so second red has probability 2/4. Multiply conditional steps: (3/5)(2/4)=3/10. Alternatively C(3,2)/C(5,2)=3/10. The answers agree because the first method considers ordered draws and the second method considers unordered pairs consistently.

sections.title: 8. Independent practice before continuing
paragraphs: Exercise A: Two fair dice are rolled. What is P(sum=9)? Answer: 4/36=1/9 because (3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3) work. Exercise B: A class contains 40% beginners and 60% advanced learners. Passing rates are 50% and 80%. Overall pass rate is 0.4×0.5+0.6×0.8=0.68. Exercise C: For 100 independent observations with population SD 20, SE of sample mean is 20/10=2. Explain each denominator before moving to the corresponding detailed lesson.

sections.title: 1. Why algebra becomes geometry
paragraphs: A scalar is one number; a vector is an ordered collection of numbers that can represent position, direction, a data record or a collection of model parameters. For a vector x=(3,4), the Euclidean norm ||x||=√(3²+4²)=5 measures length. The dot product x·y=Σx_i y_i measures alignment: positive dot products correspond to acute angles, zero to perpendicular nonzero vectors, and negative to obtuse angles. If y=(1,−2), x·y=3−8=−5. Two vectors with the same length can point in entirely different directions, so a norm and a dot product answer different questions.

Linear algebra gives us a language for transformations of entire collections of numbers. Matrix A transforms a vector x into Ax; its columns tell us what happens to basis directions. For A=[[2,0],[0,3]], a unit x-axis vector becomes twice as long and a unit y-axis vector three times as long. Multiplication of matrices composes transformations. Their order matters in general: rotating then stretching need not equal stretching then rotating. Keep the dimensions in view: an m×n matrix times an n×1 vector produces an m×1 vector.

sections.title: 2. Span, subspace, basis and dimension
paragraphs: The span of vectors is every linear combination of them. In R², the vectors (1,0) and (0,1) span the entire plane: any (a,b)=a(1,0)+b(0,1). A set is linearly independent if none of its vectors can be formed from the others. A basis spans the space and is independent; the number of vectors in a basis is its dimension. Adding (1,1) to those two basis vectors adds redundancy, not a new dimension. Vector spaces and subspaces require closure under addition and scalar multiplication and contain zero. The line x+y=0 through the origin is a subspace; the parallel line x+y=1 is not because it omits zero.

sections.title: 3. Solve equations by elimination, not memorization
paragraphs: A linear system can be written Ax=b. Gaussian elimination uses three reversible elementary row operations: swap rows, multiply a row by a nonzero scalar, and add a multiple of one row to another. The goal is row echelon form, where pivots reveal which variables are constrained. Consider x+y=3 and x−y=1: subtract the second equation from the first, yielding 2y=2, so y=1 and x=2. If elimination yields 0=1, the system has no solution. If a free variable remains and no contradiction occurs, there are infinitely many solutions over the real numbers.

The rank of A counts independent columns (equivalently independent rows). Its nullity counts the dimension of solutions to Ax=0. Rank-nullity states rank(A)+nullity(A)=n, where n is number of columns. A 3×5 matrix of rank 3 therefore has nullity 2. In data science, a null direction identifies a change in model coefficients that leaves predictions Ax unchanged, suggesting nonidentifiability or redundant features.

sections.title: 4. Determinant, inverse and eigen thinking
paragraphs: For a square 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], det=ad−bc. A zero determinant means at least one dimension collapses; the transformation is noninvertible. A nonzero determinant guarantees a unique solution to Ax=b for every b. Eigenvectors satisfy Av=λv: the matrix scales their direction by the eigenvalue λ. For diagonal matrix diag(2,−3), the coordinate axes are eigenvector directions, with eigenvalues 2 and −3. A negative eigenvalue reverses orientation along its eigenvector; eigenvalues are not always positive and need not be real for every real square matrix.

When A has a full basis of eigenvectors, A=PDP^−1 and powers become A^k=PD^kP^−1. This helps analyse repeated transitions or dynamic systems. Not every matrix is diagonalizable, so do not assume such a basis always exists. Symmetric real matrices are especially well behaved: they have real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis.

sections.title: 5. Orthogonality, projection and least squares
paragraphs: An orthogonal matrix Q satisfies QᵀQ=I and preserves Euclidean lengths. Projecting a vector onto a direction u computes ((x·u)/(u·u))u. For x=(3,4) and u=(1,0), projection is (3,0); the residual (0,4) is perpendicular to the chosen line. Projection matrices are idempotent: P²=P. Applying the same projection twice does not change the result after the first time.

Real data rarely satisfy Ax=b exactly, because observations contain noise. Least squares minimizes ||Ax−b||² and yields normal equations AᵀAx=Aᵀb when differentiable; a unique ordinary least-squares solution requires appropriate rank conditions. The residual is orthogonal to the column space: Aᵀ(Ax−b)=0. This directly connects linear algebra to linear regression.

sections.title: 6. Decompositions and matrix curvature
paragraphs: LU decomposition records Gaussian elimination as A=LU (possibly with row pivoting), enabling efficient repeated solutions of systems with the same coefficient matrix. Singular value decomposition A=UΣVᵀ applies to rectangular matrices too: U and V contain orthogonal directions and Σ nonnegative singular values. Singular values near zero indicate directions that are strongly compressed, which matters for stability, pseudoinverses and dimensionality reduction.

A quadratic form xᵀAx helps decide whether a function bends upward or downward. For a symmetric matrix with all positive eigenvalues it is positive definite; this corresponds to strict curvature of the quadratic objective. Mixed positive and negative eigenvalues yield an indefinite form and saddle-like geometry. The Hessian in multivariable optimization plays this role, although the GATE DA calculus section focuses on one variable.

sections.title: 7. Worked example: column dependence and regression
paragraphs: Suppose two columns of a data matrix are x1=(1,2,3) and x2=(2,4,6). The second is exactly twice the first. The matrix rank is one, not two. A linear prediction model w1x1+w2x2 depends only on w1+2w2, so many coefficient pairs produce identical predictions. This is why an ordinary inverse of XᵀX may not exist when features are perfectly collinear. One remedy is removing redundant columns; another is an appropriate pseudoinverse or regularization. The mathematical issue is about unique coefficients, not necessarily unique predictions.

sections.title: 8. Practice problems and reasoning
paragraphs: Exercise A: Are (1,2) and (2,4) independent? No: the second is twice the first. Exercise B: det([[1,2],[3,6]])=1×6−2×3=0, so the matrix is singular. Exercise C: A 4×6 matrix has rank 3. Nullity is 6−3=3. Exercise D: For diagonal A=diag(4,9), singular values are 4 and 9; eigenvalues are 4 and 9 here too, but their equality is a special property of this matrix, not a general rule. Work each answer without looking, then explain the geometry in words.

sections.title: 1. Functions are models of change
paragraphs: A function assigns exactly one output to each valid input. Think of f(x) as a machine: choose x, apply the rule, receive f(x). Its domain matters: 1/(x−2) is undefined at x=2; √(x+3) is real only when x≥−3. Graphs let you see trends and curvature that algebra alone can hide. In GATE questions, start by checking what input values are allowed; optimization on an interval also requires considering its boundaries.

A limit looks at what a function approaches near a point, even if the value at that point is missing or different. For f(x)=(x²−4)/(x−2), substitute x=2 gives 0/0, an indeterminate expression. Factor x²−4=(x−2)(x+2), cancel away from x=2, then take the limit: 4. This does not mean the original expression is defined at x=2. A function is continuous at c only if f(c) is defined, the limit exists, and that limit equals f(c).

sections.title: 2. Derivative means instantaneous rate
paragraphs: The derivative arises from the limit of a difference quotient: f′(x)=lim_(h→0)[f(x+h)−f(x)]/h. For f(x)=x², expanding (x+h)²−x² gives 2xh+h²; dividing by h gives 2x+h; letting h→0 gives 2x. The derivative measures tangent slope, marginal change or instantaneous speed. If f(t) is distance over time, f′(t) is instantaneous velocity under the chosen sign convention. Second derivative f″ describes how the first derivative changes and indicates local concavity.

Rules simplify routine differentiation: d(x^n)/dx=nx^(n−1), sum rule, product rule, quotient rule and chain rule. The chain rule handles composition: for f(x)=(2x+1)³, derivative is 3(2x+1)²×2=6(2x+1)². The outside derivative is not enough; include the inner derivative. In a rushed exam, annotate outer and inner functions before computing.

sections.title: 3. The mean value theorem explains average versus instant
paragraphs: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), the mean value theorem guarantees at least one c between a and b where f′(c)=[f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a). For f(x)=x² on [1,3], secant slope=(9−1)/2=4, so f′(c)=2c=4 gives c=2. Notice the conditions matter: a jump or a corner can invalidate the theorem, even when some numerical slope happens to match by accident.

The sign of derivative controls monotonicity: f′>0 means locally increasing, f′<0 locally decreasing on intervals where the sign holds. A stationary point where f′=0 might be a local maximum, minimum or neither. For f(x)=x³ at zero, f′(0)=0 but the function keeps increasing; this counters the misconception that every zero derivative marks an extremum.

sections.title: 4. Optimization is comparing candidates
paragraphs: To optimize f(x) in one variable, first identify the domain and constraints. Find interior critical points where f′=0 or f′ does not exist, then test signs or curvature. For a maximum on a closed interval, also evaluate endpoints. Consider f(x)=x² over [−2,1]. The only stationary point x=0 has f=0, but the global maximum is f(−2)=4. Stopping after solving f′=0 would miss the correct answer.

The first derivative test checks sign changes: negative→positive indicates local minimum, positive→negative local maximum. The second derivative test at a stationary point says f″(c)>0 implies local minimum, f″(c)<0 local maximum. If f″(c)=0, the test is inconclusive; inspect higher derivatives or signs. This distinction is tested frequently because it requires understanding rather than memorizing a table.

sections.title: 5. Taylor series approximates a curve near a point
paragraphs: Taylor's formula about a expresses f(x) by derivatives at a: f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+f″(a)(x−a)²/2!+... . At a=0, this is called a Maclaurin series. For e^x, all derivatives at zero are one, so e^x≈1+x+x²/2 near zero. With x=0.1 this approximation gives 1.105 instead of the exact 1.10517... . The approximation is local; as x moves far from zero, error may grow. In GATE, identify the required order and center before substituting.

sections.title: 6. Gradient descent connects derivatives to machine learning
paragraphs: A model learns parameters by minimizing a loss. One-dimensional gradient descent updates x_new=x−ηf′(x), where η>0 is the learning rate. Suppose f(x)=(x−3)² and x0=0. Derivative is 2(x−3), so f′(0)=−6. With η=0.1, x1=0−0.1×(−6)=0.6, closer to the optimum x=3. If η is too large, updates may oscillate or diverge. The update tells a story: if the slope is positive, move left; if negative, move right. But the magnitude of the step also matters.

sections.title: 7. Exam-worked case: optimize cost
paragraphs: A rectangular field must have perimeter 40 units. Let one side be x and the other be y, so 2x+2y=40 and y=20−x. Area A(x)=xy=x(20−x)=20x−x². Differentiate A′=20−2x, set zero to get x=10, then y=10. A″=−2<0 confirms a local maximum; over physical domain 0≤x≤20 endpoints give zero area, so it is global. The formula wasn't given—building the objective was the hard part.

sections.title: 8. Practise with variations
paragraphs: Exercise A: Differentiate x³−3x. Answer: 3x²−3. Stationary points x=−1,1. Exercise B: Is x³ at x=0 a local extremum? No, despite derivative zero. Exercise C: Approximate sin(0.1) using the linear Maclaurin term: 0.1; the next nonzero correction is −x³/6. Exercise D: For f(x)=−(x+2)²+5, global maximum on the real line is 5 at x=−2. Explain why the negative square cannot increase above zero.

PDSA.subject: PDSA
PDSA.title: Python, Data Structures & Algorithms: the foundations course

sections.title: 1. Learn how a program executes
paragraphs: A program is a precise sequence of operations on data. Python names such as x, price and items refer to objects; they do not permanently declare one type. The expression 5+2 produces an integer; 5/2 gives 2.5 as a float; 5//2 gives 2 as floor division; 5%2 gives remainder 1. For negative operands, flooring is toward negative infinity: −7//3=−3, not −2. The identity a=b(a//b)+(a%b) is useful for checking modulo calculations when b is nonzero.

Python core data types include int, float, bool, str, list, tuple, set and dict. Strings and tuples are immutable; lists, dictionaries and sets are mutable. Mutation changes an existing object, whereas creating a new object and rebinding a name is different. This distinction appears in code-output questions. For example, a=[1,2]; b=a; b.append(3) makes a equal [1,2,3] because two names refer to the same list. But b=a.copy() creates a shallow copy that initially contains the same elements without sharing the top-level list.

sections.title: 2. Control flow and functions
paragraphs: An if/elif/else chooses one path based on conditions. for iterates over a sequence or range; while repeats until its condition becomes false. range(2,9,3) produces 2,5,8: start included, stop excluded, step positive three. In nested loops, trace the outer loop and count inner iterations carefully; this directly feeds time complexity analysis.

Functions separate input, operation and output. Their parameters are local names, and return gives a value back to the caller. Recursion means a function calls itself; correct recursion needs a base case and a recursive step that moves toward that base case. For factorial: fact(0)=1, fact(n)=n×fact(n−1) when n>0. For n=4, calls unfold as 4×3×2×1=24. Draw the call stack to understand memory use: depth n usually needs O(n) stack frames.

sections.title: 3. List indexing and slicing without guessing
paragraphs: Python uses zero-based indexing. If a=[10,20,30,40,50], a[0]=10, a[-1]=50 and a[1:4]=[20,30,40]. The syntax a[start:stop:step] picks indices beginning at start but excludes stop. a[::-1] returns a reversed copy; it does not reverse a in place. List comprehensions compactly express loops, but GATE code-output questions often combine a comprehension with a condition. Rewrite it as an explicit loop if needed.

Use sets for uniqueness and membership, dictionaries for key-value lookup, stacks for last-in-first-out work and queues for first-in-first-out work. Hash-table-based dictionary and set operations often have average O(1) lookup, but adversarial collisions can worsen performance. Do not confuse average with guaranteed worst case.

sections.title: 4. Big-O: count operations, not seconds
paragraphs: Big-O describes how time or space grows with input size n. A single loop through n elements is O(n). Two consecutive n-loops take O(n)+O(n)=O(n), not O(n²); two nested n-loops generally take O(n²). Halving a search interval repeatedly takes about log₂n stages. Constants matter in real systems, but asymptotic analysis ignores fixed factors for large n. Big-O is an upper bound; Θ gives a tight bound when known.

Binary search is O(log n) only because the input is sorted and one comparison lets you discard half the remaining elements. Linear search may need O(n) comparisons but does not require sorted data. Insertion sort is O(n²) worst case yet O(n) best case on already sorted data; merge sort reliably uses Θ(n log n) comparisons with extra memory, while quicksort has average Θ(n log n) time but worst-case Θ(n²) for poor pivots. A comparison-based sorting algorithm cannot do better than Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case over unrestricted orderings.

sections.title: 5. The data-structure choice changes the algorithm
paragraphs: Arrays allow O(1) indexed access and typically O(n) insertion in the middle due to shifting. Singly linked lists require O(n) traversal to reach the kth item but can insert after a known node in O(1). Stacks serve bracket matching, undo and DFS. Queues serve arrival order and BFS. Trees represent hierarchy; balanced binary search trees have O(log n) lookup, but a completely skewed BST can require O(n). Make operation-by-operation comparisons rather than claiming a structure is "faster" in general.

Graph G=(V,E) describes vertices and edges. Adjacency lists use O(V+E) memory for ordinary graph representations, while adjacency matrices use O(V²). BFS uses a queue and visits nodes by increasing number of hops, so it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS uses recursion or a stack and explores deep paths before backtracking; it is useful for cycle detection and topological sorting. Dijkstra's algorithm handles nonnegative weighted shortest paths using the smallest current tentative distance. A negative edge invalidates the usual Dijkstra correctness argument.

sections.title: 6. Detailed trace: binary search
paragraphs: Given a=[2,5,7,11,15,19,23], find 15. Initialize low=0, high=6; mid=(0+6)//2=3, value a[3]=11. Since 15>11, set low=4. New mid=(4+6)//2=5, value=19; since 15<19 set high=4. Now mid=4, value 15: found in three comparisons. The algorithm discards portions only because the list is sorted. An off-by-one error happens when low/high updates fail to exclude the old midpoint or when loop conditions mishandle an empty range.

sections.title: 7. Detailed trace: BFS versus DFS
paragraphs: For edges A–B, A–C, B–D and C–E, BFS starting A enqueues B,C, then D,E. One possible discovery order is A,B,C,D,E. Recursive DFS in alphabetical neighbour order may visit A,B,D, then backtrack, then C,E, yielding A,B,D,C,E. Both visit reachable vertices; only BFS gives shortest-hop distances from A without extra weights. The precise DFS order can vary with neighbour iteration order, so read that assumption in questions.

sections.title: 8. Practice set with solutions
paragraphs: Exercise A: What is list(range(5,0,−2))? Answer: [5,3,1]. Exercise B: Code runs for i in range(n), then for j in range(n). Complexity is O(n), not O(n²), when loops are sequential. Exercise C: A complete undirected graph of six nodes has 6×5/2=15 edges. Exercise D: Dijkstra is not applicable to arbitrary negative-weight graphs; choose a suitable alternative such as Bellman–Ford when negative weights are present and no negative cycle makes the desired distance undefined. After reading, practise tracing code by hand before running it.

sections.title: 1. Data needs structure before it needs queries
paragraphs: A database stores data together with rules for describing, searching and updating it. Imagine a college: students enroll in courses, courses have instructors, and each enrollment may have a grade. If you put everything into one giant spreadsheet, student names and course titles repeat, updates become inconsistent, and the same fact may be entered differently. Database design starts with identifying real entities (Student, Course), attributes (student_id, course_name), and relationships (Enrollment connects Student to Course). An ER diagram is a conceptual model; relational tables are a logical model implementing it.

Cardinality matters. One student may enroll in many courses and one course may have many students: a many-to-many relationship. Create Student(student_id,...), Course(course_id,...) and Enrollment(student_id,course_id,grade). Enrollment uses two foreign keys referencing the parent tables, and its composite primary key may be (student_id,course_id) when repeated enrollments are prohibited. A key identifies a record. A candidate key is minimal and unique; a primary key is the selected candidate key; a foreign key expresses a reference constraint. Every key rule should correspond to a business rule, not merely to accidental uniqueness in today's sample.

sections.title: 2. Think of relational algebra as operations on tables
paragraphs: Selection σ filters rows by a condition; projection π retains a set of columns. A join combines rows satisfying a relationship; Cartesian product produces every pair of rows and can grow very quickly. For Employees(name,dept_id,salary), the algebra π_name(σ_salary>50000(Employees)) means filter high earners, then return their names. Relational algebra describes operations; tuple relational calculus describes which tuples satisfy a logical formula. Understanding both makes SQL more predictable.

sections.title: 3. SQL execution stages and NULL
paragraphs: A standard SELECT query can contain FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY and LIMIT. Logical query processing filters rows in WHERE before aggregation, groups surviving rows, filters groups in HAVING, then projects results. Write: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM Employee GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*)>5; using COUNT(*) in WHERE would be wrong. This logical order matters more than the order in which keywords appear in a query.

SQL NULL means unknown or missing, not zero or an empty string. Comparisons to NULL return UNKNOWN rather than TRUE/FALSE, so use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. Aggregate COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) ignores NULL values in that column. An INNER JOIN retains matching rows; LEFT JOIN also returns unmatched left rows with NULL for right columns. A WHERE predicate on a right-side field after a LEFT JOIN can inadvertently eliminate unmatched rows and change the intended result.

sections.title: 4. Nested queries, EXISTS and relational logic
paragraphs: Consider finding customers who have never ordered anything. A robust query is SELECT c.id FROM Customer c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id);. The correlated subquery is checked relative to each customer. EXISTS cares whether at least one row satisfies the condition, not about the actual SELECT expression. NOT IN can behave surprisingly when the subquery includes NULL, because SQL's three-valued logic may prevent rows being selected. Practice drawing two tiny sample tables by hand to understand joins and subqueries.

sections.title: 5. Normalization and functional dependencies
paragraphs: A functional dependency X→Y means rows agreeing on X must agree on Y. For example, course_id→course_name expresses that one course ID determines one course name. If a table also stores every enrollment, course_name repeats across students; renaming a course requires multiple updates. Such structures suffer update, insertion and deletion anomalies. Normal forms separate facts according to dependencies. First normal form treats values as atomic according to the chosen model; second and third normal forms reduce particular partial or transitive dependency problems; BCNF is stricter by requiring determinants of nontrivial dependencies to be superkeys. The practical goal is consistent data, not satisfying a formula without considering real semantics.

sections.title: 6. Physical storage and indexes
paragraphs: A heap file stores records in no particular key order, which suits some inserts but often forces scans for lookups. A sorted file supports range access but insertion can be costly. A hash index efficiently targets equality searches under suitable assumptions, whereas a B+ tree preserves key order, supports range scans and uses linked leaves. An index consumes space and slows some writes because it must be maintained. For query `WHERE amount BETWEEN 100 AND 200`, a B+ tree is usually a better fit than an ordinary hash index. For `WHERE id=42`, both may be useful depending on the system and workload.

sections.title: 7. Transactions and ACID
paragraphs: A transaction groups related updates into one logical unit. Atomicity means all-or-nothing, consistency means declared constraints are maintained, isolation controls interference among concurrent transactions, and durability means committed updates survive failure under the system's guarantees. Suppose a transfer subtracts ₹100 from A and adds ₹100 to B: failure after the first write must not leave a partial transfer committed. Isolation prevents races such as two concurrent updates overwriting each other. Different isolation levels make different tradeoffs, and not every database guarantees serializable execution by default.

sections.title: 8. Warehousing is for analysis rather than transactions
paragraphs: Operational databases optimize current records and frequent small updates. A warehouse organizes historical data for summarization. A star schema places a central fact table around denormalized dimensions; a snowflake schema normalizes dimension hierarchies further. In a sales warehouse, FactSales stores measures such as quantity and revenue with keys to Date, Product and Store dimensions. Roll-up aggregates cities to states or months to quarters; drill-down moves toward detail. A data cube represents measures across dimensions. Additive measures such as total units can sum across many dimensions; nonadditive ratios like average price should be recomputed as numerator/denominator after aggregation, not added.

sections.title: 9. Data preprocessing belongs to the data story
paragraphs: Before modeling, inspect types, missingness, unusual values, scaling and the meaning of each column. Normalize may mean schema normalization in databases or numeric scaling in machine learning; never confuse them. Standardization uses (x−mean)/SD; min-max uses (x−min)/(max−min). Discretization creates bins, sampling selects observations, and compression trades size against information, depending on whether it is lossless. Fit transformation parameters on training data only; applying test statistics during training leaks information about held-out data.

sections.title: 10. Practise SQL reasoning
paragraphs: Exercise A: Why can `LEFT JOIN` return NULL? The left row may have no matching right row. Exercise B: `COUNT(*)` versus `COUNT(salary)` when salary is NULL? First counts the row, second does not. Exercise C: For customers with zero orders, choose `NOT EXISTS` correlated by customer ID. Exercise D: A monthly average price should be computed using total sales divided by total units, not by summing daily averages. Explain the data grain and denominator for every aggregation.

sections.title: 1. Learning from examples means generalizing
paragraphs: Machine learning constructs a rule from observations instead of encoding every decision by hand. A row of data contains features X; supervised learning additionally has a target y. Regression predicts a number, classification predicts a category or probability, and unsupervised learning seeks structure when labels are unavailable. The purpose is generalization: accurate predictions on new observations from an appropriate distribution. High training accuracy alone does not establish that property. A model can memorize the training set and fail on unseen data.

Split data before model selection. A training set fits parameters; validation data help choose hyperparameters and detect overfitting; a separate test set estimates final performance once. In k-fold cross-validation, divide training data into k subsets, train on k−1 and validate on the remaining subset, rotating k times. Leave-one-out CV uses one validation example per fold. For time-ordered data, random shuffling may leak the future; use splits respecting time. For grouped observations from the same person or machine, separate groups when that matches deployment requirements.

sections.title: 2. Objective functions tell the model what success means
paragraphs: For regression, mean squared error is average (prediction−truth)² and strongly penalizes large errors. Mean absolute error is average absolute error and is less sensitive to some outliers. Classification commonly uses cross-entropy to reward calibrated probability assigned to correct labels. Training minimizes an objective based on error and sometimes a regularization term. The optimizer does not automatically understand fairness, reliability or business costs; these must be reflected in data, evaluation or the task formulation.

Simple linear regression models ŷ=β0+β1x. Intercept β0 is predicted y at x=0, if meaningful; slope β1 is prediction change per unit x. For multiple linear regression, ŷ=Xβ with row-wise features. Given full column rank and standard least-squares assumptions, β̂=(XᵀX)^−1Xᵀy; otherwise use appropriate decompositions or pseudoinverses. Ridge adds λ||β||², discouraging extreme coefficients and reducing sensitivity to correlated inputs. It introduces bias deliberately in exchange for potentially improved stability and generalization.

sections.title: 3. Optimization: gradients are directions, not magic
paragraphs: To minimize loss L(w), gradient descent updates w_new=w−η∇L(w). Positive derivative points uphill, so subtracting it goes downhill for sufficiently small steps near a smooth region. Learning rate η too large can overshoot or diverge; too small can train slowly. Feature scaling changes curvature and therefore step behaviour. Derive one update manually before using code: if L(w)=(w−4)², w0=0 and η=0.1, gradient −8 gives w1=0.8. Repeated steps approach 4 under suitable learning rate.

sections.title: 4. Classification: probabilities, decisions and confusion matrices
paragraphs: Logistic regression takes a linear score z=w·x+b and maps it to probability p=1/(1+e^(−z)). A classification threshold converts p into a decision. Changing the threshold changes precision and recall without changing the fitted probabilities. A confusion matrix counts true positive (TP), false positive (FP), false negative (FN) and true negative (TN). Precision=TP/(TP+FP) asks whether predicted positives are reliable. Recall=TP/(TP+FN) asks how many real positives were found. Accuracy=(TP+TN)/N can mislead when one class dominates. F1 balances precision and recall through their harmonic mean. State which class is "positive" before calculation.

sections.title: 5. Compare different classifier assumptions
paragraphs: k-nearest neighbours predicts from nearby training examples and is sensitive to distance metric and scale. Naive Bayes combines prior P(class) with feature likelihoods while assuming conditional independence between features given class; it can work surprisingly well despite imperfect assumptions. Linear discriminant analysis usually models class-conditional distributions with a shared covariance matrix, producing linear decision boundaries. Support vector machines seek a large separating margin, using slack penalties when perfect separation is impossible and kernels for suitable nonlinear boundaries. Decision trees split features according to impurity reduction; they are interpretable but deep trees may overfit. A strong exam answer distinguishes each algorithm's assumptions, decision mechanism and failure cases.

sections.title: 6. Bias, variance and validation
paragraphs: A very simple model may consistently miss important patterns: high bias, or underfitting. A very flexible model may change dramatically with training samples: high variance, or overfitting. Training loss usually decreases as complexity increases, but validation loss can eventually rise. Cross-validation helps choose model complexity on a fair basis. Use an untouched final test set after completing this search. Don't assume "high model accuracy" means success if labels are imbalanced, data are leaking, or training and deployment populations differ.

sections.title: 7. Neural networks: compose weighted transformations
paragraphs: A neuron computes z=w·x+b followed by activation a=φ(z). Nonlinear activation such as ReLU(z)=max(0,z) lets multiple layers learn nonlinear relationships; a stack of purely linear layers still acts as one linear transformation. A feedforward network maps input features through hidden layers to outputs. For a 4→5→2 network, weights total 4×5+5×2=30, plus biases 5+2=7 if each non-input neuron has one. Backpropagation efficiently applies the chain rule from output loss backward through layers, delivering gradients used by the optimizer. It's differentiation of a composed function, not a separate mysterious learning rule.

sections.title: 8. Unsupervised learning: clusters and principal components
paragraphs: Clustering groups examples by a similarity rule without known targets. k-means alternates assigning each sample to nearest centroid and recomputing cluster means; it tends to prefer roughly spherical groups under Euclidean distance and can depend on initialization. k-medoids uses actual observations as representatives and works with broader dissimilarities. Hierarchical clustering creates nested clusters: agglomerative merges from individual samples, divisive splits from one group. Single linkage uses closest inter-cluster pair; complete linkage uses farthest inter-cluster pair. They respond differently to chains of nearby points.

Principal component analysis (PCA) rotates centered data to orthogonal directions of decreasing variance. Eigenvectors of covariance give principal directions; eigenvalues measure variance along them. If eigenvalues are 9 and 1, first component explains 9/(9+1)=90% of total variance. PCA is unsupervised: greatest variance is not necessarily greatest power to predict a target. Standardization can change PCA results by changing feature scales. Check what objective an exam question actually specifies before choosing PCA or a supervised technique.

sections.title: 9. Integrated example: classify fraud alerts
paragraphs: A fraud detector flags 100 transactions: 30 are actually frauds (TP) and 70 are legitimate (FP). It missed 20 other fraud transactions (FN). Precision=30/(30+70)=0.30 and recall=30/(30+20)=0.60. If reviewing flagged transactions is costly, low precision matters; if missed fraud is costly, recall matters. A lower alert threshold tends to increase recall but may reduce precision. The choice is a business decision informed by the confusion matrix, not merely the highest possible overall accuracy.

sections.title: 10. Test your explanation
paragraphs: Exercise A: MSE for y=[2,5], predicted=[3,3] is (1²+2²)/2=2.5. Exercise B: For a binary classifier TP=20, FP=5, FN=15, compute precision=20/25=0.8 and recall=20/35≈0.571. Exercise C: With eigenvalues 4,3,3, two PCA components retain 7/10=70% variance. Exercise D: Training accuracy near 100% but validation accuracy poor suggests overfitting, not confirmed good performance. For each question, identify the model assumption before calculating.

sections.title: 1. What does an intelligent agent actually do?
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence studies systems that represent situations, choose actions, search for outcomes, reason from knowledge and handle uncertainty. A useful starting model is an agent: it observes information about an environment, maintains some representation of the situation, and selects actions to achieve a goal. In an exam search problem, formalize the state space, initial state, allowable actions, transition model, goal test and path cost. An apparently simple puzzle can become a search problem containing thousands of states if your state representation includes unnecessary details.

For route planning, a state can be the current location, an action can be travelling along a permitted road, and a path cost can be travel time. A path is a sequence of actions linking the start to a goal. Search algorithms differ in how they choose the next frontier state. Their guarantees depend on assumptions: completeness means finding a solution if one exists under specified conditions; optimality means finding a least-cost solution under specified assumptions. Always ask whether weights are uniform, positive, or potentially negative.

sections.title: 2. Uninformed search: frontier order changes everything
paragraphs: Breadth-first search (BFS) processes frontier states in first-in-first-out order using a queue. It expands depth 0, then depth 1, then depth 2, so it finds a shortest path by number of edges when each move has equal cost. Its memory can grow exponentially with depth in a branching tree. Depth-first search (DFS) uses recursion or last-in-first-out stack behaviour and goes deep before backtracking. It often uses less memory than BFS in tree-search settings but may miss shallow solutions for a long time; in infinite spaces without repeated-state handling it may not terminate.

Uniform-cost search (UCS) uses a priority queue ordered by accumulated path cost g(n), so it generalizes BFS when edge costs differ. If A→B cost 1, B→G cost 10, and A→G cost 5, UCS prefers the direct cost-5 path even though the two-edge path initially looks tempting. A cost of 1+10=11 is not improved by taking more edges. With nonnegative costs and appropriate handling, UCS finds a least-cost goal. Beware confusing the cheapest *frontier node so far* with the final cheapest solution before goal selection.

sections.title: 3. Informed search: estimate the distance to the goal
paragraphs: A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost from n to a goal. Greedy best-first search prioritizes h(n) and can be misled because it ignores cost already spent. A* uses f(n)=g(n)+h(n), combining known past cost and estimated future cost. An admissible heuristic never overestimates true remaining cost; a consistent heuristic also satisfies a triangle-like inequality h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′). These properties support optimality guarantees under the appropriate A* variant.

Suppose node X has g=4 and h=3, so f=7; node Y has g=6 and h=0, so f=6. A* expands Y first if both are in the priority queue. This does not mean Y has the cheaper route *so far*; it has the cheaper combined estimate. A heuristic of zero everywhere reduces A* to uniform-cost search. Recognize what changes when h is informative, inadmissible or inconsistent.

sections.title: 4. Adversarial search: plan against another decision-maker
paragraphs: In games like tic-tac-toe, each player's move changes the next player's options. Minimax models alternating MAX and MIN players with evaluation values at leaf states. MAX chooses a move with the highest guaranteed outcome assuming MIN acts optimally. Suppose two branches lead to MIN leaves [3,8] and [5,6]. MIN returns 3 from the first and 5 from the second; MAX chooses the second branch because its guaranteed value 5 is larger. It's a recursive calculation, not a guess at the opponent's personality.

Alpha-beta pruning avoids exploring subtrees that cannot change the minimax result. Alpha tracks the best guaranteed value for MAX along the path; beta tracks an upper bound imposed by MIN. When alpha≥beta, a branch can be skipped because it cannot improve the relevant choice. Move ordering affects how much pruning happens, but correct alpha-beta produces the same minimax value as full search. Practice drawing a three-level tree and propagating min/max numbers before learning shortcuts.

sections.title: 5. Propositional logic: exact meanings of AND, OR and implication
paragraphs: A proposition is a statement with a truth value. The connectives ¬, ∧, ∨ and → build more complex statements. p→q is logically equivalent to ¬p∨q; it is false only when p is true and q false. This truth-functional implication does not by itself imply causation. De Morgan's laws say ¬(p∧q)≡¬p∨¬q and ¬(p∨q)≡¬p∧¬q. Build truth tables rather than relying on English intuition for compound expressions.

A knowledge base (KB) entails a claim α when every model in which KB is true also makes α true. If KB contains P and P→Q, then Q follows via modus ponens. Entailment describes the semantic relationship; an inference rule is a syntactic way to derive conclusions. Soundness means inferred claims are entailed; completeness (relative to a logic) means entailed claims can be inferred. Keep the difference between "the knowledge is true" and "the reasoning procedure proves it" clear.

sections.title: 6. First-order logic adds objects and quantifiers
paragraphs: Propositional logic treats whole statements as indivisible symbols; first-order logic adds predicates about objects and quantifiers ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists). Quantifier order is essential. ∀x∃y Loves(x,y) says everyone loves someone, possibly a different person each time. ∃y∀x Loves(x,y) says one particular person is loved by everyone. These are not equivalent. Negating ∀xP(x) gives ∃x¬P(x); negating ∃xP(x) gives ∀x¬P(x). Practice translating sentences into formulas and back into ordinary language to avoid scope errors.

sections.title: 7. Reasoning under uncertainty with Bayesian networks
paragraphs: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph encoding dependencies among random variables. Each node has a conditional probability distribution given its parents. For a chain A→B→C, the joint distribution factorizes as P(A)P(B|A)P(C|B). The graph also encodes conditional independences: in the chain, A and C are conditionally independent given B under the network Markov assumptions. In a fork A←B→C, conditioning on common parent B blocks the path between children; in a collider A→B←C, conditioning on B can *open* a path between parents. This collider behaviour surprises beginners and is highly testable.

Exact inference can sum out hidden variables. For example, P(C)=Σ_a Σ_b P(a)P(b|a)P(C|b). Variable elimination combines factors and sums out hidden variables strategically; elimination order can greatly affect intermediate table size. Approximate inference uses sampling, such as drawing observations from the network and estimating event proportions. For 230 successes among 1000 independent samples, probability estimate is 0.23 and sampling error decreases as effective sample size grows. Sampling trades exactness for feasible computation on large networks.

sections.title: 8. An integrated planning example
paragraphs: A delivery robot starts at S, can move to A at cost 2 or B at cost 5, then can reach G from A at cost 6 or from B at cost 1. BFS sees both S→A→G and S→B→G as two-edge paths and may return the first, costing 8. Uniform-cost search compares total costs and chooses S→B→G at cost 6. With a valid heuristic, A* can guide the same optimal decision while exploring fewer nodes. This example shows why the problem's cost definition, not an algorithm's name alone, determines the correct method.

sections.title: 9. Independent questions and answers
paragraphs: Exercise A: The path cost g=3 and heuristic h=4 give A* priority f=7. Exercise B: A consistent heuristic must satisfy h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′). Exercise C: Negation of "Every student passed" is "At least one student did not pass." Exercise D: For A→B→C, conditioning on B blocks the A–C trail. Exercise E: If a game MIN node has leaf scores 2,9 and 6, its value is 2. Draw state graphs and truth tables rather than memorizing words alone.

sections.title: 1. General aptitude is not a memory test
paragraphs: General Aptitude contributes 15 marks to GATE and rewards accurate language, numerical reasoning, interpretation and spatial thinking. The aim is to translate an unfamiliar-looking question into a small number of clear operations. Use a three-pass approach: identify what is being asked, extract given data and constraints, then check the answer against units, reasonableness and the options. Spending 30 seconds creating a table or sketch can save several minutes of arithmetic.

sections.title: 2. Verbal ability begins with the sentence's logic
paragraphs: For grammar, first identify the true subject and predicate. "The list of errors is long" uses singular *is* because subject is list, not errors. Verb tense should respect chronology; pronoun references should have clear antecedents; articles depend on pronunciation as well as spelling (an honest mistake, a university). In vocabulary questions, read the entire sentence and note whether the surrounding argument suggests a positive, negative or neutral meaning. Do not rely exclusively on a memorized word list without context.

Reading comprehension separates explicit facts from inferences. If a passage says "Some models need more data," then "All models need more data" does not follow. An inference must be supported by the given text, not just plausible from general knowledge. Narrative sequencing uses introduction before reference: a sentence with "this" or "it" often depends on something introduced earlier. Track chronology, cause-and-effect and contrast markers such as however, therefore and subsequently. For argument questions, distinguish necessary conclusion from a tempting overgeneralization.

sections.title: 3. Ratios, proportions and percentages
paragraphs: A ratio 2:3 means two equal-sized parts versus three parts, with total five parts. If 250 items are split 2:3, groups contain 100 and 150. Percentage is a denominator-specific proportion multiplied by 100. Growth from 200 to 260 is (260−200)/200×100=30%, not 60/260. For sequential percentage changes, use multipliers: +20% then −20% gives 1.2×0.8=0.96, an overall 4% decrease. Percentage-point changes are different: an accuracy increase from 70% to 80% is ten percentage points, or about 14.3% relative increase.

Weighted averages matter when groups differ in size. If 20 students average 60 marks and 30 average 80, the overall mean is (20×60+30×80)/50=72, not the unweighted average 70. Use alligation or ratio shortcuts only after confirming the quantities are comparable. Always label units and group counts; many data-interpretation errors come from mixing thousands with lakhs or percentages with absolute totals.

sections.title: 4. Powers, logarithms, number patterns and counting
paragraphs: Exponent rules include a^m×a^n=a^(m+n), (a^m)^n=a^(mn), and a^0=1 for a≠0. A logarithm reverses an exponent: log₂32=5 because 2^5=32. For real-valued logs, the argument must be positive and the base positive and not one. Use these restrictions when solving log equations.

For sequences, test simple first differences, second differences, ratios and alternating subsequences. The series 2,6,12,20,30 has differences 4,6,8,10, so next is 42. Counting questions require choosing between multiplication for sequential slots and combinations for unordered selections. Five distinct people can fill president and secretary positions in 5×4=20 ways, but two-person committees can be chosen in C(5,2)=10 ways. Always ask whether order matters, repetition is allowed and zero may lead a numeric code.

sections.title: 5. Geometry, elementary statistics and visual data
paragraphs: Know perimeter and area for rectangles, triangles and circles; surface area and volume for standard 3D solids; the Pythagorean theorem; and basic angle relations. Scaling lengths by k multiplies areas by k² and volumes by k³. An object doubling in side length becomes eight times the volume, not twice. For data interpretation, read axis scales, units, legends and denominators. A bar graph with truncated axes can visually exaggerate small differences; numerical answers must come from values, not visual impression.

Elementary statistics covers mean, median, range and basic probabilities. Outliers pull means more than medians. For fair independent dice, probabilities are counted over ordered pairs; for a bag with 3 red and 2 blue balls, one uniformly drawn ball is blue with probability 2/5. Probability language "at least one" often becomes a complement. Read whether a chart gives counts, rates or cumulative totals before making comparisons.

sections.title: 6. Reasoning: distinguish necessary facts from possibilities
paragraphs: Deduction guarantees conclusions from premises, while induction suggests general patterns from observed cases. The statement "All doctors are graduates; Riya is a doctor" logically entails "Riya is a graduate." The converse "All graduates are doctors" does not follow. Arrangement puzzles benefit from grids that record fixed and forbidden positions. For A left of B and B left of C, infer A before C through transitivity. Do not assume people are adjacent unless the question explicitly says so.

sections.title: 7. Spatial aptitude needs deliberate sketches
paragraphs: Rotation changes orientation by an angle; reflection flips handedness; translation shifts position without turning; scaling changes size. Mark one asymmetrical feature on a shape before mentally rotating or mirroring it. For paper folding and cutting, reverse the folds one at a time, reflecting the punched location across each fold line. If a page is folded in half once and a hole is punched away from the fold, unfolding produces two mirrored holes. If the punch is exactly on the fold, the count changes. Small details in the diagram determine the correct result.

sections.title: 8. Worked example: mixtures and weighted averages
paragraphs: A store sells 10 units at ₹20 and 30 units at ₹40. Average selling price per unit is total revenue divided by total units, not (20+40)/2. Revenue=10×20+30×40=1400; units=40; average=₹35. This is weighted averaging by quantity. If an exam asks for overall percentage growth across two departments, compute combined base and final totals first and then apply the percentage formula; averaging individual growth rates is generally wrong.

sections.title: 9. Mini-test with explanations
paragraphs: Exercise A: After +25% and −20%, the multiplier is 1.25×0.8=1, so no net change. Exercise B: A cube of side 3 has volume 27; doubling its side gives volume 216, eight times. Exercise C: Average of 3,3,4,10 is 5, median is 3.5. Exercise D: "A few students passed" cannot establish "Every student passed." Exercise E: Two fixed roles filled from six people without repetition yield 6×5=30 assignments. Explain why each denominator or multiplication rule is correct before checking the answer.
